newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani committee suggests cutting import tariff.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani committee suggests cutting import tariff.

text.p: A tariff reform committee appointed by Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif has proposed slashing import duties and general sales tax.
The committee also said in a seven-page report, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters, that no questions should be asked on sources of investment for a five-year period.
It recommended cutting the tariff on finished goods to 45 percent from 65 percent and setting a maximum rate of five percent on primary raw material.

"The (maximum tariff) rate should be reduced to 35 percent by the year 2000," said the report, submitted to the government on Thursday. "The rationalisation of tariff and trade liberalisation will spur production and boost exports."
Sharif, who took office last month, had asked the 25-member committee of businessmen, industrialists and officials to identify tariff-related problems and suggest solutions.
The report said investors should not be quizzed on the source of their funds. "No question should be asked regarding industrial investment and capital up to year 2002."
It proposed a five-year reform plan backed by constitutional protection. "No executive order should overrule constitutional provisions guaranteed under the tariff reform package."
It said general sales tax should be reduced to 10 percent in the budget for fiscal 1997/98 (July-June) from the present 15 to 23 percent, and cut to seven percent by the year 2002.
"The sales tax is exorbitant and would prevent the documentation of the economy," the report said.
It argued that in principle sales tax and excise duty should not be imposed on the same products simultaneously.

"The present dual customs valuation system (should) be abolished...and replaced with the GATT code of valuation from July 1, 1997 under the WTO (World Trade Organisation) agreement signed by Pakistan," it added.

It said import duty on industrial plants and machinery not manufactured locally should not be more than five percent while imports of second-hand machinery should be allowed duty-free. "Regulatory duty on all imports should be withdrawn," it said.
The report expressed concern over "excessive taxes and levies" on the food and beverage and soap industries.
It criticised the new government's decision to open a nothing-to-declare green channel at airports to allow Pakistanis to bring in goods without customs inspection or payment of duty.
The report said "unscrupulous elements" were abusing the facility, which it said should be reserved for Pakistanis who were returning after spending at least six months abroad.
